key_insight: Parents and pediatric staff are more willing to use AI when the condition seems more serious, but trust drops when data sharing feels too broad or AI conflicts with clinicians.
clinical_relevance: For pediatric AI to be adopted in routine care, systems should be tailored to the scenario, make privacy protections clear, and define how human and AI recommendations will be reconciled.
method: Surveyed parents in two cohorts (n=198; n=79) and pediatric healthcare professionals (n=33)
Compared willingness to use AI across diagnosis, treatment, and disagreement scenarios
Assessed predictors including data privacy preferences, AI knowledge, and perceived disease severity
evidence_signal: Cross-sectional survey data showed that more liberal data privacy was associated with lower willingness to use AI (p<.001), and higher perceived disease severity increased willingness in one parent cohort (β=.10, p=.013).
watch_item: Findings are preference-based and scenario-specific, so real-world adoption may differ when AI performance, workflow burden, and accountability rules are explicitly defined.
paper_title: Acceptability of AI-applications in routine clinical care for children and adolescents: perspectives of parents and healthcare professionals
